power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. info.title: When an integration composite fails to cohere: host-language orientation as social-world affiliation, and the formative logic behind a failed scale An explanatory sequential mixed-methods study of international students in Japan

author.affiliation:
Center for the Study of International Cooperation in Education (CICE)
								Hiroshima University
								
									Higashi-Hiroshima
									Japan

text.text: Surveys often treat international students' host-language use and "integration" items as measures of one disposition.
This article asks what such items measure, and what it means when they fail to cohere.
It draws on an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study at a national research university in Japan during the shift to online teaching.
The data are a survey of international students (N = 176) and 39 interviews with 40 students.
Choice of the Japanese survey form was the outcome.
Region of origin dominated that choice (Sinosphere odds ratio ≈ 16.2).
Three integration indicators were small, could not be separated from origin, and did not cohere (alpha = 0.36).
The interviews suggest that the indicators are formative traces of a clustered social world, not reflections of one trait.
For such indicators, internal consistency is the wrong test.
A low alpha should prompt the question of what the items jointly index.
Survey research often treats international students' use of the host language, and their "integration" more broadly, as a proxy for acculturation.
It measures them with self-report items such as daily language use, use of institutional systems, and living arrangement.
These items are assumed to capture one underlying disposition.
The practice is standard and has a sound basis: interview language has a long record as an acculturation proxy (Lee, Nguyen and Tsui 2011).
text.formatted: The practice is standard and has a sound basis: interview language has a long record as an acculturation proxy <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Lee, Nguyen and Tsui 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers rarely ask what these items actually measure.
When the items predict an outcome, what do they predict through?
When they fail to cohere, what does that failure tell us?
The case is a survey of international students at a large national research university in Japan.
It was conducted after teaching moved online during the COVID-19 pandemic, and it is paired with interviews from the same population and period.
The survey produced a clear and, at first, disappointing pattern.
Region of origin was by far the strongest predictor of whether a respondent chose the host-language (Japanese) version of the form.
Form choice is treated here as a behavioral indicator of host-language orientation.
Both versions reached every invitee through the same channel, so the choice was the respondent's own.
Theory would expect three integration-type indicators to matter: daily host-language use, student-portal use, and private residence.
Each added only small predictive power that depended on the model.
All three lost significance once origin was tightly controlled, and together they did not form a reliable composite.
Taken alone, the survey cannot say whether these items measure anything apart from origin.
The easy conclusion is that origin determines orientation and the items are noise.
That conclusion would be a mistake, and this paper shows why.
The measurement literature already warns against it.
Language-use items tend to track origin and ethnicity instead of forming a separate component (Teruya and Pan 2021).
text.formatted: Language-use items tend to track origin and ethnicity instead of forming a separate component <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Teruya and Pan 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Apparent structure among acculturation dimensions can be an artifact of scale format (Kang 2006).
text.formatted: Apparent structure among acculturation dimensions can be an artifact of scale format <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Kang 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Acculturation domains also do not measure the same way across origin groups (Kwok 2023).
text.formatted: Acculturation domains also do not measure the same way across origin groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kwok 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A strong demographic predictor next to weak, incoherent mechanism items is therefore a pattern to explain, not a defect to patch.
Explaining it requires asking the students themselves.

The paper uses an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design and integrates the two strands through a joint display and a metainference (Creswell and Plano Clark 2018; Fetters, Curry and Creswell 2013).
text.formatted: The paper uses an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design and integrates the two strands through a joint display and a metainference <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Creswell and Plano Clark 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Fetters, Curry and Creswell 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Two research questions structure the study.
RQ1.
Among international students, what predicts host-language orientation?
Do integration-type indicators (daily host-language use, student-portal use, residence type) predict it independently of national origin?
RQ2.
Do those indicators cohere as a measure of a construct distinct from origin?
If not, what does the failure of coherence signify?
The paper addresses three specific problems.
First, it identifies what host-language orientation indexes.
The answer is neither proficiency nor nationality.
It is the social world a student is affiliated with: co-national, host-institutional, mixed-international, or, under rupture, none.
This settles a question the language-as-proxy literature leaves open.
Second, it gives a reading rule for a common and misread result.
An integration composite that fails an internal-consistency test may be formative, not defective.
Interview evidence can show which.
If it is formative, the usual remedy narrows the construct: dropping the indicator that does not correlate.
Third, it gives an inference rule for a common pattern in which a demographic marker dominates an outcome while mechanism items predict weakly.
In that pattern the marker bundles mechanisms the items capture only in part, and other methods can recover them.
A companion paper develops the substantive account of how these social worlds are produced and bounded.
The measurement argument made here does not depend on it.
>Background
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Background</head>

text.text: Survey research has a long practice of reading acculturation from language. Lee, Nguyen and Tsui (2011) showed that interview language works as a usable proxy for acculturation among Asian Americans in a population-based survey.
text.formatted: Survey research has a long practice of reading acculturation from language. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Lee, Nguyen and Tsui (2011)</ref> showed that interview language works as a usable proxy for acculturation among Asian Americans in a population-based survey.

text.text: Foreign-born respondents interviewed in English resembled US-born respondents more closely than those interviewed in another language.
This precedent makes the language of a survey form readable as an acculturation signal.
The closest study to the present one is Saavedra Cisneros (2025).
It treats the choice and switching of interview language in Spanish-English bilingual surveys as a symbolic act that reflects identity as well as acculturation.
The present paper shares that premise, with three differences.
The outcome here is the choice of a written form, not a switch during an interview.
The setting is Japan.
And the choice is read as indexing social-world affiliation, not identity. Kato (2018) adds a caution.
text.formatted: And the choice is read as indexing social-world affiliation, not identity. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Kato (2018)</ref> adds a caution.

text.text: In that study, the effect of interview language on self-rated mental health was explained by proficiency and ethnic identity together.
The signal is real but confounded.
This work leaves two questions open: what the proxy stands for (competence, identity, or social position), and how such items behave once combined into a composite.
Two studies carry most weight for this paper. Kang (2006) showed that the apparent lack of independence between cultural-orientation dimensions is partly an artifact of scale format.
text.formatted: Two studies carry most weight for this paper. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kang (2006)</ref> showed that the apparent lack of independence between cultural-orientation dimensions is partly an artifact of scale format.

text.text: The cause is paired items in a frequency format.
A composite can therefore fail to cohere because of how its items are built, even when the underlying phenomenon is coherent.
The most direct support comes from the systematic review by Schumann and colleagues (2020) of acculturation measurement in epidemiological research.
It finds wide inconsistency in how the construct is operationalized.
It concludes that proxies such as language skills and feeling of belonging should be measured on their own, without being combined into a score.
This paper reaches the same practical conclusion from a different literature and on different grounds.

Recent psychometric work on the most widely used bidimensional instrument shows the same weakness from the inside. Testa and colleagues (2019) found that the Vancouver Index of Acculturation's two-factor structure held, but its items differed in how hard they were to endorse. O'Donald and Calia (2026) tested it on a UK-based East Asian sample and found poor fit for the original structure.
text.formatted: Recent psychometric work on the most widely used bidimensional instrument shows the same weakness from the inside. <ref type="bibr">Testa and colleagues (2019)</ref> found that the Vancouver Index of Acculturation's two-factor structure held, but its items differed in how hard they were to endorse. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">O'Donald and Calia (2026)</ref> tested it on a UK-based East Asian sample and found poor fit for the original structure.

text.text: The mainstream-orientation factor had weak and mostly non-significant loadings, while the heritage factor held.
In that sample the host-orientation side breaks down, and that is the side the present indicators tap.
This critique is best placed against the framework the word "integration" comes from.
Berry's acculturation model classifies people by their orientation to the heritage culture and to the host culture (Berry 1997).
text.formatted: Berry's acculturation model classifies people by their orientation to the heritage culture and to the host culture <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Berry 1997</ref>).

text.text: Crossing the two gives integration, assimilation, separation, and marginalization.
Instruments in that tradition, such as the Vancouver Index of Acculturation (Ryder, Alden and Paulhus 2000), measure each orientation as a reflective scale.
text.formatted: Instruments in that tradition, such as the Vancouver Index of Acculturation <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Ryder, Alden and Paulhus 2000)</ref>, measure each orientation as a reflective scale.

text.text: Its attitude and behaviour items are expected to cohere.
The present paper does not reject that framework.
It makes a narrower claim about the framework's behavioural residues.
A survey not designed to measure attitudes may keep only a few situational items: daily language use, use of institutional systems, and residence.
These items are parts of a social-world ecology, not expressions of an attitude, so the expectation of internal consistency does not carry over.
A "failed" integration composite may fail only as a reflective scale while remaining valid as a formative index.
The usual operationalizations of the fourfold model do not draw this distinction. Jang, Park, Chiriboga and Kim (2017) add that English-only surveys carry an upward selection bias.
text.formatted: The usual operationalizations of the fourfold model do not draw this distinction. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Jang, Park, Chiriboga and Kim (2017)</ref> add that English-only surveys carry an upward selection bias.

text.text: For this study the upshot is clear.
The survey's use of language and integration items is standard practice.
Yet the literature that supports the proxy also predicts that such items will track origin and will not cohere into a clean latent construct.
The quantitative strand reports this same pattern, and the qualitative strand is used to explain it.
A closely related study, Ranabahu and De Silva (2024), develops a typology of intergroup and intragroup contact for the acculturation of international students in Japan.
text.formatted: A closely related study, <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Ranabahu and De Silva (2024)</ref>, develops a typology of intergroup and intragroup contact for the acculturation of international students in Japan.

text.text: The companion paper engages it on the substantive mechanism.
The present paper asks the prior question: what a non-cohering composite of such indicators means as measurement.
Interpretation turns on the distinction between reflective and formative measurement models.
The distinction is long established in psychometrics and structural-equation modeling, but rarely applied to acculturation and integration composites.
In a reflective model, items are manifestations of one underlying latent variable.
The latent variable causes the item responses, so the items should covary.
Internal-consistency statistics such as Cronbach's alpha are then the right test of whether the items hang together.
In a formative model the direction of causality is reversed.
The items cause or make up the construct, and the construct is the aggregate they produce.
Such indicators need not covary.
They may correlate weakly or even negatively and still each contribute validly to the composite (Bollen and Lennox 1991).
text.formatted: They may correlate weakly or even negatively and still each contribute validly to the composite <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bollen and Lennox 1991)</ref>.

text.text: The consequences for measurement practice are direct and central to this argument. Bollen and Lennox (1991) show that the conventional wisdom equating good measurement with high interitem correlation holds only for reflective (effect) indicators.
text.formatted: The consequences for measurement practice are direct and central to this argument. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bollen and Lennox (1991)</ref> show that the conventional wisdom equating good measurement with high interitem correlation holds only for reflective (effect) indicators.

text.text: Applying internal-consistency criteria to causal (formative) indicators is a category error.
It can lead a researcher to discard valid items because they do not correlate. Diamantopoulos and Winklhofer (2001) turn this point into a procedure for building indices.
text.formatted: It can lead a researcher to discard valid items because they do not correlate. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Diamantopoulos and Winklhofer (2001)</ref> turn this point into a procedure for building indices.

text.text: For a formative composite, indicators should be chosen for how well they cover the construct's facets, not by internal-consistency or item-total statistics.

Dropping a formative indicator that does not correlate changes the meaning of the construct instead of improving its reliability. Edwards and Bagozzi (2000) state the general point: the relation between constructs and measures can run in either direction and must be specified on substantive grounds.
text.formatted: Dropping a formative indicator that does not correlate changes the meaning of the construct instead of improving its reliability. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Edwards and Bagozzi (2000)</ref> state the general point: the relation between constructs and measures can run in either direction and must be specified on substantive grounds.

text.text: The formative model has strong critics. Howell, Breivik and Wilcox (2007) show that the meaning of a formative construct can shift with the outcomes used to estimate it.

text.text: Items that do not covary may be causal indicators of a latent variable, composite indicators that only form an index, or covariates.
Subject knowledge must decide which.
The argument here does not depend on that choice.
Under each reading, the three items should not be summed into one scale and judged by alpha.
They are best read one at a time, as this paper does.
In the present case, daily host-language use, use of an institutional portal, and residence type are unlikely to be three expressions of one latent "integration" trait that causes all three.
They are three partly independent facets of a student's living situation, and together they make up a socialworld ecology.
A student can use the portal daily without living in a private residence.
A student can also live privately while conducting daily life in a co-national language.
If the items are formative, the expectation that they should cohere rests on the category error Bollen and Lennox describe, and so does the disappointment when they do not.
This literature offers acculturation research no worked example of a formative integration composite.
Nor does it offer a method for recovering what the indicators jointly index.
The present study supplies that case.
It pairs the failed composite with interview evidence of what each item indexes, and so turns a psychometric problem into a substantive result.
>Methodology
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Methodology</head>

text.text: The study uses an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design (Creswell and Plano Clark 2018).
text.formatted: The study uses an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Creswell and Plano Clark 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The quantitative strand is analyzed first.
It establishes a pattern that it cannot interpret by itself.
The qualitative strand is then analyzed to explain that pattern.
The problem sets this order.
The survey shows that one variable dominates respondents' language behavior, while the theoretically motivated "integration" indicators predict weakly, unstably, and without cohering.
The instrument cannot settle what the behavior indexes.
The interviews are therefore analyzed to recover what the instrument missed.
The two strands are integrated through a joint display.
Each quantitative finding is set beside the qualitative mechanism that bears on it, with an explicit judgment of fit (Fetters, Curry and Creswell 2013; Guetterman, Fetters and Creswell 2015).

text.text: The strands rest on separate samples with no case linkage.
Integration is therefore claimed only at the level of population inference and complementarity.
No statement in this paper links an individual survey respondent to an individual interviewee.
Three conditions support reading the interviews as explaining the survey pattern.
First, the samples share one context: one institution, one population, and one period, the COVID-era shift to online teaching.
Second, the interviews were held while the survey was still open (interviews 11 February to 2 March 2021; survey 13 February to 31 March 2021).
No survey result existed when they were conducted, so the survey could not steer them.
The design is sequential in analysis, not in collection.
Third, the qualitative coding was finished before integration and independently of it, so the fit judgments are not circular.
This supports a population-level inference, not case-level causal attribution: the mechanisms recovered from the interviews account for the shape of the survey pattern.
Data were collected among international students at the host institution, a large national research university in Japan.
Collection took place while teaching had moved online in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
The survey and interview data come from a larger project on international students' experiences in this period.
Earlier analyses of the same dataset addressed cultural adaptation through a phenomenological lens (Zhang 2025) and student retention through a social-capital framework (Zhang 2026).

text.text: A companion paper, currently under review, develops the substantive account of how host social worlds are produced and bounded.
The present study does not re-present those analyses.
It re-reads the survey around a distinct measurement question: what host-language orientation indexes, and what a non-cohering integration composite signifies.
It pairs this with a reading of the interviews for that purpose.
The survey was completed by 177 international students.
One response was excluded as internally inconsistent: it reported undergraduate enrolment at the host institution together with residence in a dormitory in China.
This left an analytic sample of 176.
Of these, 133 chose the host-language (Japanese) form and 43 the English form.
Invitations went mainly by group email to the enrolled international-student population, supplemented by participant referral.
Both language versions appeared together in every invitation, so each recipient was offered both and chose which to open.
Form choice is therefore a selection between two available options.
It is not an artifact of which version reached whom.
Referral recruitment means the sample is not a probability sample ( §5.3), but referrals circulated the paired instrument, not one version alone.
The dependent variable was choice of the host-language form, taken as a behavioral indicator of host-language orientation.
Two features limit what it can carry.
First, no standardized proficiency measure was collected.
The reading of form choice as orientation, and not as reading ability, is therefore not tested against a criterion within the survey.
Second, the choice is between two written forms.
A rival reading is that respondents open whichever language is cheaper to read.
Origin bundles reading cost almost as tightly as any social variable, since Sinosphere students read written Japanese at a discount through shared kanji.
The survey cannot decide between the two readings, which is why the qualitative strand is needed.
Section 5.1 sets out the interview evidence that favors the affiliation reading and explains why the measurement argument holds under either reading.
The principal predictor was country or region of origin.
It was entered both as full categorical origin and as a higher-order Sinosphere grouping.

Alongside it were three integration-type indicators that prior literature treats as proxies for acculturation or host engagement: self-reported daily use of the host language, frequency of student-portal use, and residence type.
Residence was coded as private residence, meaning any dwelling other than an institutional dormitory or share house.
Six respondents, all from China, were still living in their family home outside Japan, and their residence is treated as missing.
This leaves 139 private residents among 170 respondents.
Analysis proceeded in four steps.
First, logistic regression estimated the association between each predictor and host-form choice.
Second, because origin produced quasi-complete separation, models were re-estimated with Firth's penalized-likelihood logistic regression.
This is the standard remedy for separation and small-sample bias (Firth 1993; Heinze and Schemper 2002).
text.formatted: This is the standard remedy for separation and small-sample bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Firth 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Heinze and Schemper 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Third, robustness was tested with stratified models and with within-origin nonparametric comparisons (Mann-Whitney U) inside the largest single-origin subgroup.
One stratification addresses a distinct threat.
For students in an English-medium programme, opening the English form may be an institutional default, not an expressive choice.
Twenty respondents were in that track: 13 chose English and 7 the host-language form.
Thirty of the 43 English-form choices came from outside the track, so track scripting cannot carry the outcome.
The stratified estimates in §4.1 use the 156 respondents outside the track.
As a benchmark, five background covariates (age, gender, level of study, part-time work, and monthly living cost) were run through the same three specifications (Supplementary Table S2).

text.text: Fourth, the internal consistency of the three indicators as a candidate composite was assessed with Cronbach's alpha (Cronbach 1951).

text.text: Because the composite did not cohere, the indicators are reported and interpreted one by one.
Analyses were carried out in Python with NumPy.
Firth's estimator was implemented directly, with profile penalized-likelihood confidence intervals and penalized likelihood-ratio p-values.
The qualitative corpus comprised 40 international students across 39 recorded interviews; one interview was held jointly with two participants.
The interviews took place between 11 February and 2 March 2021, mostly by video call.
Twenty-four were held in Mandarin, ten in Japanese, and five in English.
An external transcription service transcribed 33 interviews in 2021.

For this study, 24 recordings, including the other six, were also transcribed with automatic speech recognition (OpenAI Whisper; Radford et al. 2023), run locally so that this step sent no audio outside the research team.

The transcripts were then verified and, where needed, corrected and translated.

The semi-structured interviews covered the participant's path into study in Japan, changes to study and daily life under online teaching, social contact and relationships, language use across settings, views of the host society, and future plans.
Transcripts were analyzed with reflexive thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke 2006).

It attended to variation within origin groups as well as across them.
A systematic check for disconfirming cases was run for the companion paper's mechanism and is reported there (see §5.3).
In this paper the qualitative material serves one purpose: to identify what each of the survey's integration items indexes.
The companion paper develops the full analysis of how social worlds are produced and bounded.

text.text: The integrative claim is a meta-inference across the rows.
The quantitative pattern and the qualitative account reconcile once host-language orientation is read as an index of social-world affiliation, not of proficiency or nationality.
The three integration indicators are treated as formative, not reflective.
This has two consequences for the analysis.
First, they are not summed or averaged into a single scale score.
They are entered one at a time, so each keeps its own coefficient and its own relation to origin.
Second, their internal consistency is reported (Cronbach's alpha), although formative indicators are neither expected nor required to cohere.
The low alpha is what the paper sets out to reinterpret.
It is reported as the thing to be explained, not as a reliability check passed or failed.
Two properties make this value even less informative.
It rests on only three items, and alpha rises mechanically with the number of items.
It also spans different types of item, and alpha's assumptions rarely hold even for similar items (McNeish 2018).
McNeish also warns against citing such problems to excuse a low alpha.
The argument therefore rests on the direction-ofcausality specification, not on the size of the coefficient.
That specification makes internal consistency the wrong criterion whatever its value.
The formative reading is an interpretive claim grounded in the interview evidence; a formal model is left to future work ( §5.3).

>Findings

text.text: Of the 176 respondents, 133 chose the host-language (Japanese) form and 43 the English form.
The choice was concentrated by origin before any modelling (Figure 2).

text.text: Of the 114 Sinosphere respondents, 106 chose the host-language form.
Non-Sinosphere respondents split the other way, 27 to 35.
Region of origin dominated the outcome by an order of magnitude.
The Sinosphere grouping had an odds ratio near 16.2 (95% CI [7.2, 40.3], p < .001), and China and Taiwan stood at 14 to 16 times a pooled non-Sinosphere reference.

text.text: The intervals are wide because origin nearly separates the outcome.
This is acute for Taiwan, where all five respondents chose the host-language form.
These estimates are best read as order-of-magnitude effects, not precise values.
Against this, the three integration-type indicators were small.
Their significance depended entirely on how finely origin was modelled (Table 1; Figure 1).

text.text: Unadjusted, only private residence reached significance (OR ≈ 3.10, p = .007).
Net of the coarse Sinosphere grouping, private residence and daily use were nominally significant.
Net of full categorical origin, none was.
These estimates support a claim of non-separability, not of inertness.
Once origin is modelled at full resolution, no indicator keeps an effect that can be told apart from the origin ecology it sits in.
Private residence keeps OR ≈ 2.48 on an interval of [0.74, 7.90].
The model spreads the cases across 25 origin categories, and eighteen hold one or two respondents.
The construction of the origin variable does not drive this.
Treating the two case-variant entries for one origin separately gives 26 categories and moves no integration estimate by more than 0.06.
A formative reading predicts this non-separability for indicators that trace a clustered ecology.
The finer the origin control, the less of each indicator can be identified apart from origin.
One counter-movement supports the same reading.
Daily use is more significant net of the coarse grouping (OR ≈ 1.55, p = .034) than unadjusted (OR ≈ 1.34, p = .12).
This is the suppression pattern expected when a crude control separates out part of a mixed ecology.
Tight conditioning agrees.
Outside the English-medium track (n = 156), the Firth daily-use p = .69; within China, the Mann-Whitney p = .98.
Of five background covariates, part-time work kept its effect net of full origin (OR ≈ 3.46 [1.23, 11.1], p = .018).
Age, gender, and living cost were not significant in any specification.
Level of study lost its unadjusted effect once origin was entered (Supplementary Table S2).

text.text: The model can detect an effect beyond origin, and the integration indicators do not show one.
The inference rests on robustness across nine indicator-byspecification tests, not on any single p-value.
As a candidate composite, the indicators did not cohere (Cronbach's alpha = 0.36, n = 168).
Pairwise Spearman correlations were weak and uneven (daily use with portal use ρ = .32, daily use with residence ρ = .09, portal use with residence ρ = .04).
This is the low and uneven association expected of formative indicators that tap distinct facets.
It is not the pattern expected of reflective expressions of one latent trait.
As §3.6 notes, the argument does not rest on the size of this coefficient.
The survey alone cannot decide whether the integration items measure a construct distinct from origin.
The qualitative strand is brought in to explain the pattern.

The interviews supply the construct that reconciles the two strands.
Host-language orientation indexes neither proficiency nor nationality as such.
It indexes which social world a student is affiliated with: a co-national world, a host-national or host-institutional world, a mixed international world, or, under rupture, none.
The typology has a lineage.
The functional model of sojourner friendship networks distinguishes co-national, host-national, and multinational networks with distinct functions.
It treats orientation toward each network, not proficiency, as the substantive variable (Bochner, McLeod and Lin 1977; replicated by Furnham and Alibhai 1985).

text.text: The companion paper develops the model's mechanisms and presents the full set of cases.
Here, three observations from the corpus show what the construct is.
They also show why it, and not proficiency or nationality, is what the survey's dependent variable reads.
First, the clearest case is one in which language and social world come apart completely.
A participant from China about to begin doctoral study (#11, interviewed in Mandarin; paraphrased) had a mixed circle of co-national and Japanese classmates before the pandemic.
Small talk before class and in the seminar made her feel that she existed in the school and in society.
It connected her to people (~21:27, ~21:32).
When classes moved online, she lost that circle, not her language ability: 「不管是说中⽂还是说⽇语，就是什么都说不了」 (~18:48).
Apart from her partner, she met no one to talk to, in Chinese or in Japanese.
The companion paper analyses the same case for a different question.
If host-language use measured proficiency, her Japanese use should have been unaffected.
It collapsed because the world it indexed collapsed.
Second, the corpus spans the full typology, and language tracks the world in every cell.
Among co-nationals, social life reproduces itself in the co-national language (#29, in Mandarin).
One participant pursues a deliberate project of self-fashioning toward the host (#5, in Mandarin).
Another defaults to the family language at home, and both Japanese and English fade from disuse (#44a, in Japanese, ~11:00).
In each case the reported language pattern makes sense as affiliation and does not make sense as proficiency.
Third, one structural fact about the corpus makes the point without relying on any testimony.
One interview was conducted in Japanese between two international students of different national origins, with Japanese as their shared medium.
There, host-language use marks membership in a mixed international world whose common language is Japanese.
A social-world reading predicts this, and a nationality reading cannot account for it.
(This rests on the medium of the interview, not on a participant's statement.)
The formative reading predicts that each indicator tracks a different facet of the clustered ecology described in §4.2.
This explains why the indicators align with origin, the marker of that ecology, while failing to correlate with one another.
Daily host-language use indexes affiliation, not skill.
The cases in §4.2 show the dissociation directly.
Host-language use rises as an identity project for #5.
It fades to disuse in #44a's household and co-national world.
It collapses for #11 when her classes move online, though her competence is unchanged.

The sociolinguistic and bicultural-cognition literatures predict this for an affiliative signal, as opposed to a competence signal (Myers-Scotton 1993; Hong, Morris, Chiu and Benet-Martínez 2000; Luna, Ringberg and Peracchio 2008).

text.text: One case anchors the point in objective terms.
A participant from Taiwan holds the highest certification, JLPT N1 (#1, in Mandarin).
She rated her own Japanese as poor (~17:08) and described herself as only living in Japan, not blended in: 「仅仅是在这⾥⽣活，但是并没有融⼊到他们」 (~21:26).
Certified competence and host belonging came apart in the same person.
Certification was recorded for only two participants, so this case is an existence proof, not distributional evidence.
Residence type, the largest single coefficient, is best read as a proxy, not as a cause in its own right.
It bundles two things: who is positioned for host contact, and who is supported in it.
A private residence usually routes a student into host-society daily life instead of a co-national dormitory world.
It also correlates with the disposition and support that turn positioning into contact.
Because it bundles both, it carries more signal than the other two indicators but is the hardest to read as a single mechanism.
That is the profile of a formative indicator that aggregates several facets.
The different social profiles of dormitory and private-residence students in this dataset are analysed elsewhere (Zhang 2025; Zhang 2026).

text.text: The point here concerns only what residence type does as an indicator.
Portal use indexes routing into host-institutional systems specifically, as against conducting institutional life through co-national peers.
It is the thinnest of the three indicators.
Much institutional information reaches students through informal co-national translation, not the official portal.
The indicator therefore captures only the part of institutional engagement that runs through the host-language channel.
Portal engagement in this population was low and largely peer-mediated, as reported from the same dataset elsewhere (Zhang 2025; Zhang 2026).
These are three partly independent facets of a living situation, not three expressions of one disposition.
A student can score high on one and low on another without contradiction.
This is why internal consistency is low, and why that value says little about validity (Bollen and Lennox 1991).

The data show no sign of a shared latent "integration" trait.
Joint-display integration.
Fit: expansion and clarification.
This is the reconciling step of the paper.
Origin dominance seems to conflict with interviewees' insistence that origin does not shape their integration.
The conflict disappears once the dependent construct is read as socialworld affiliation.
Origin clusters with that ecology and so carries the population signal.
The mechanisms that produce social worlds sit outside the survey, which leaves the integration items small and incoherent.

>Discussion
text.formatted: <head n="5." >Discussion</head>

text.text: Read on its own, the quantitative result invites a flat interpretation.
Origin dominates, the integration-type indicators add little, and the composite does not cohere.
The interviews show why that reading is wrong.
The resolution, and the answer to RQ1, is to read the dependent variable as social-world affiliation, not as proficiency or nationality.
Once host-form choice is understood as an index of that affiliation, the strands stop conflicting.
Origin predicts strongly at the population level because it travels with social world, contact ecology, and language environment.
It bundles the very mechanisms the interviews isolate case by case ( §4.2, §4.3).
At the individual level, affiliation is produced by a contact ecology that the survey items tap only in part.
Daily use reads affiliation, not skill.
Residence bundles positioning with support, and portal use captures only the institutional life that runs through the official channel.
That is why the integration coefficients range from 1.18 to 3.54 while origin sits near 16, and why alpha is 0.36.
The quantitative result is not overturned but re-specified.
Nationality is a marker of clustered conditions, not a cause.
RQ2 asked whether the indicators cohere.
They do not, for two reasons.
First, the measurement literature predicts as much (Teruya and Pan 2021; Kang 2006; Kwok 2023; Schumann et al. 2020).
text.formatted: First, the measurement literature predicts as much <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Teruya and Pan 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kang 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Kwok 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Schumann et al. 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Second, and more specifically, the three items are formative indicators of a clustered ecology.
Internal consistency is the criterion for reflective scales.
It does not apply to indicators that cause the construct and need not correlate.
A low alpha here is expected by construction.
It calls for a closer look at the items, not for their removal.
One rival to the affiliation reading must be answered, because on the survey alone it fits the numbers as well.
The outcome is a choice between two written forms.
The origin effect could therefore reflect the relative cost of reading Japanese versus English, not any social orientation.
Reading cost is bundled by origin just as social world is.
The interviews add a pattern that the reading-cost account does not predict.
Host-language use in daily life rises and falls with a student's social world while proficiency stays constant.
It also dissociates from formal certification in at least one case (#1, JLPT N1 yet little host-language life).
For the central thesis the question can stay open.
Under either reading, the outcome is a formative trace of an ecology bundled by origin.
The methodological contribution is the one named in §1.
A low alpha on an "integration composite" should prompt the question of what the items jointly index, not a search for a cleaner scale.
Acculturation proxies are often combined into a single score (Schumann et al. 2020).
text.formatted: Acculturation proxies are often combined into a single score <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Schumann et al. 2020</ref>).

text.text: Such scores are then judged as reflective scales.
This case shows what that habit costs.
It turns a signal into an apparent defect.
It sends the researcher looking for better items when the items were already reporting something.
The case also shows how to recover the signal: by putting the question to the population the instrument was measuring.
The conditions that call for this reading can be stated in three parts.
A demographic marker dominates an outcome by an order of magnitude (origin at OR ≈ 16).
Mechanism items predict weakly and unstably (unadjusted ORs of 1.20 to 3.10, losing significance under conditioning).
And a composite fails internal consistency (alpha = 0.36).
Where a survey shows this pattern, discarding the items throws information away.
Treating the marker as the cause mistakes a proxy for a cause.
A third route reads the marker as a bundle of mechanisms and the incoherence as a signal.
It then recovers those mechanisms by other means.
Three implications follow for acculturation research.
First, composites of living-situation and language-use items should be specified as formative, because their indicators cause the construct instead of expressing it.
Second, indicators should be selected for content coverage, not itemtotal correlations.
Dropping an indicator that does not correlate narrows the construct instead of improving it (Diamantopoulos and Winklhofer 2001).
text.formatted: Dropping an indicator that does not correlate narrows the construct instead of improving it <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Diamantopoulos and Winklhofer 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Third, a strong demographic predictor beside weak formative indicators should be read as bundling mechanisms that the indicators capture only in part.
This matters in practice.
An explanation lodged in nationality points interventions at groups.
An explanation lodged in contact ecology points them at conditions that institutions control.
Several limitations bound the argument.
The strands rest on separate samples with no case linkage, so integration supports population-level inference but not case-level linkage.
The paper does not fit a formal formative measurement model; a larger, purpose-built dataset could.
No standardized proficiency measure was collected.
The affiliation reading therefore rests on the interviews, and the written-form choice cannot be separated from the relative reading cost of the two languages ( §3.3, §5.1).
A design that controls for proficiency would rule out that rival.
Participation was voluntary, and recruitment combined institutional email with referral, so the sample is self-selected.
The availability of an English form may itself shape who responds (Jang et al. 2017).
text.formatted: The availability of an English form may itself shape who responds <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Jang et al. 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The interviews were not designed around the survey items, so they bear on each item only indirectly.
A systematic search for disconfirming cases was run for the companion paper's mechanism, not for the measurement claims made here.
Finally, the data are a crosssectional snapshot under pandemic conditions and are now several years old.
Their age bounds the empirical case but not the argument.
The formative critique applies to integration composites fielded in any period.
Two directions follow.
Measurement work could treat a non-cohering composite as a question, not a flaw, and specify such composites formally as formative, for example in a multipleindicators multiple-causes model.
The substantive account of how these social worlds are produced and bounded, developed in the companion paper, could be tested with a longitudinal or case-linked design.
The broader lesson is a habit of reading.
A composite that fails to cohere has not necessarily failed.
Sometimes a demographic marker dominates while the mechanism items beside it stay small and incoherent.
The marker may then carry mechanisms those items catch only in part.
The useful response is to go and find them.
